title: Multimodal VAEs for diabetes representation learning
summary: Two variational autoencoders trained on 380,000 patient-days of continuous glucose data, testing whether adding insulin and wearable signals produces a better representation than glucose alone.
context: Coursework project for a Probabilistic & Generative ML course (MSc), data from MetaboNet, a public harmonised dataset consolidating 21 Type 1 diabetes clinical studies

sections.heading: The problem
body: Diabetes care gets assessed in snapshots — HbA1c every few months, a clinical review here and there — but a patient's metabolic state is actually changing hour by hour. I wanted to see if unsupervised representation learning could organise patient-days by how metabolically similar they are, with zero clinical labels, and whether adding insulin and wearable physiology on top of glucose actually gives you a richer picture or not.

sections.heading: Approach
body: I started with a CGM-only convolutional VAE as a baseline, then built a multimodal version that fuses three modalities — glucose, insulin, wearable physiology — through a Product-of-Experts layer. That layer combines each modality's posterior into one shared latent distribution and handles missing modalities without any extra work, which mattered a lot since wearable data only existed for a small slice of patients.

Training used 379,849 patient-days from 13 studies, evaluated on 69,894 held-out days across 305 patients. Posterior collapse was the main thing fighting me during modelling — I dealt with it using a 32-dimensional latent space, KL annealing, and a per-dimension free-bits threshold.

sections.heading: Result
body: Both models landed on the same clinically interpretable axis on their own — one latent dimension that correlates strongly with time-in-range and inversely with mean glucose, and neither model ever saw a clinical label during training.

What the multimodal model didn't do was clearly beat the baseline. Its patient-centroid distances lined up worse with glucose-derived clinical metrics (+0.448 vs +0.593 on time-in-range). I could have left it there, but I wanted to know why. Turns out every evaluation metric was derived from CGM in the first place, so they were always going to favour the CGM-only model. On top of that, insulin reconstruction fell apart on sharp bolus events — MSE loss just rewards predicting the average, and a spike isn't the average.

sections.heading: What the loss curves didn't show
body: A few early models had perfectly healthy-looking train and validation curves while being completely broken underneath. None of it showed up in the loss — I only caught it by digging into the actual reconstructed traces, the per-dimension KL values, and the latent structure itself.
list: One decoder was only reconstructing the first few hours of each day
One checkpoint got selected before the KL term even kicked in — good reconstruction loss, but a totally unregularised latent space
The insulin encoder turned out to be partly responding to a normalisation artefact
